title: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act
official_title: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act
summary: The SBIR and STTR programs are the federal government's primary mechanism for funding early-stage technology research at small businesses — agencies with large R&D budgets must set aside a percentage for competitive grants to startups, covering everything from initial feasibility through full development and commercialization. This law extends those programs through fiscal year 2031 and adds a significant national security layer: agencies must now screen all applicants against eight federal watchlists for foreign adversary connections, can deny grants based on classified intelligence, and must notify rejected applicants of the basis for denial when doing so won't compromise national security.
brief: Extends SBIR and STTR small-business research grants through FY2031 and adds mandatory screening against eight federal watchlists for foreign adversary ties.

top_lines.headline: Extended Through FY2031
subs: SBIR and STTR programs reauthorized through fiscal year 2031
New strategic breakthrough allocations added — Phase II awards for critical technology areas requiring matching funds

top_lines.headline: Eight-Watchlist Security Screen
subs: Applicants checked against UFLPA, OFAC Chinese Military-Industrial Complex, Section 889, Chinese Military Companies, Military End User, Entity, FCC Equipment, and CBP Withhold Release Orders lists
Classified security risks are also a basis for denial; rejected applicants must be notified of the basis unless doing so would compromise national security

top_lines.headline: Caps and Commercialization
subs: Maximum number of proposals per small business per fiscal year established for Phase I and Phase II
Expanded Phase III commercialization training required for agency contracting officers

likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 13, 2026 as Public Law 119-83.

items.main: Names the Act the “Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Requires federal agencies administering SBIR and STTR programs to evaluate whether applicants present security risks, including through coordination with the intelligence community, law enforcement, and other counterintelligence capabilities.
items.detail: Agencies must deny applications from small businesses with a security risk connecting them to entities or individuals on any of eight federal watchlists: the UFLPA Entity List (DHS), the OFAC Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies List (Treasury), the Section 889 Prohibition List (DoD), the Chinese Military Companies List (DoD), the Military End User List (Commerce), the Entity List (Commerce), the FCC Equipment and Services List, or the CBP Withhold Release Orders and Findings List. Classified security risks and agency-determined security risks are also grounds for denial. Upon denying an application on security grounds, the agency must notify the small business of the determination and its basis, to the extent doing so does not compromise national security. Denial on security grounds does not bar the business from applying in a subsequent award cycle.

sections.label: Section 3 — Phase II Strategic Breakthrough Funding

items.main: Creates a strategic breakthrough allocation letting agencies (with an SBIR expenditure above $100M) award up to $30M in Phase II funds per small business, drawn from up to 0.50 percent of the agency's extramural R&D budget.
items.detail: Amends Section 9 of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 638) subsections (aa) and (ff). Recipients must hold a prior Phase II award, demonstrate at least 100 percent matching funds, and show an effective technology. Total period of performance capped at 48 months; agencies must complete awards within 90 days of receiving a proposal. Briefings to the Small Business and Science committees required within 60 days of enactment. Under subsection (d), this section and its amendments cease to have effect September 30, 2031.

items.main: Requires each agency's SBIR/STTR program director to set, equally for all small businesses, a cap on the number of Phase I and Phase II proposals a business may submit per fiscal year (by fiscal year, solicitation, or topic basis).
items.detail: Adds new subsection (aaa) to 15 U.S.C. 638, effective for fiscal year 2027 and after. Topic-by-topic waivers allowed only for time-sensitive, urgent topics, capped at 5 percent of an agency's topics per fiscal year, with written justification and 15-day approval. Limit must be set no later than 90 days before the start of each fiscal year.

items.main: Directs the SBA Administrator, with the Secretary of Defense and GSA Administrator, to establish training for contracting officers and the agency acquisition workforce on Phase III SBIR/STTR awards.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638 subsections (e), (r), and (mm). Training covers SBIR/STTR missions and authorities, use of Phase III agreements, Phase III data rights, and Phase III sole source award contracts. Adds a definition of “agency acquisition workforce.”

items.main: Directs procurement center representatives to advocate for maximum practicable use and transition of SBIR/STTR products to Phase III, and requires simplified, standardized procedures and model contracts for Phase I, II, and III awards.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638(j)(4) and (r)(4). The SBA Administrator must modify the relevant policy directives within 1 year of enactment. Agencies must also issue standardized solicitation provisions and contract clauses on Phase III eligibility.

sections.label: Section 7 — Technical and Business Assistance Improvements

items.main: Lets SBIR/STTR award recipients choose their technical and business assistance (adding cybersecurity assistance and foreign-involvement screening), and lets businesses use the funds to hire or augment staff.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638(q). Sets per-project assistance amounts of not more than $6,500 for Phase I and not more than $50,000 for Phase II. Adds new subsection (bbb) requiring agencies with an I-Corps program to offer participation in I-Corps teams courses or bootcamps to SBIR/STTR recipients.

sections.label: Section 8 — Improving SBIR and STTR Data Collection

items.main: Adds award-type fields to the SBIR database and requires GSA to update the Federal Procurement Data System to flag award designations (direct-to-Phase II, subsequent Phase II, strategic breakthrough, Phase III prime/subcontract).
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638(k)(1) and section 1122(a)(4) of title 41. Also requires reporting on whether non-SBIR contracts use SBIR/STTR-funded technology and that contracting officers reference an SBIR/STTR contract ID number for prior relevant work.

sections.label: Section 9 — Extending SBIR and STTR Authorization

items.main: Extends SBIR and STTR program authorization from September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2031 and lets agencies carry over unspent fiscal year 2026 SBIR/STTR funds into fiscal year 2027.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638 subsections (m) and (n)(1)(A), striking “September 30, 2025”/“2025” and inserting “September 30, 2031”/“2031.”

sections.label: Section 10 — Extension of SBIR and STTR Programs and Activities

items.main: Extends numerous SBIR/STTR pilot programs and activities through September 30, 2031 (or fiscal year 2031), and repeals the GAO mandate in section 5142 of the FY2012 NDAA.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638 subsections (cc), (gg)(7), (hh)(2)(C), (jj)(7), (mm)(1), (qq)(3)(I), (uu)(3), (vv)(3)(C), (yy)(2), (zz)(3), plus section 851(e) of the FY2020 NDAA. Phase Flexibility (cc) is also expanded to add the Department of Energy and NASA and to cover the STTR program. Strikes section 5142 (15 U.S.C. 638a) of Public Law 112-81.

underreported.summary: Agencies may deny SBIR/STTR applications based on a security risk whose primary source is classified, without being required to disclose the basis for denial.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's security screening is presented as a watchlist-based transparency mechanism. The classified-source denial pathway allows rejection without any meaningful notification — the agency's only obligation is to tell the applicant a determination was made, not why, leaving the small business with no basis to challenge or cure the disqualification.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Van Duyne
featured_quotes.text: we must pass S. 3971 to ensure that Federal investment yields results for our country.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Lofgren
featured_quotes.text: For more than 40 years, and Small Business Innovation Research Program (SBIR), and later its companion program the Small Business Technology Transfer Program (STTR), have been contributing to U.S. leadership in technological innovation through support for small business research and development. I have had a front-row seat to the explosive growth of entrepreneurship in Silicon Valley over my lifetime. I understand well the importance of innovative small businesses to our local economy and to the U.S. economy.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Houlahan
featured_quotes.text: For years, I proudly led the bipartisan RAMP for Innovators Act, a bill that gives our small businesses the tools they need to turn great ideas into market-ready products. Today, I am thrilled that a significant portion of that work is included in the Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act. Thanks to this bill, these very important provisions and improvements will soon be law. Today's passage is a testament to what bipartisan and bicameral collaboration can achieve.

gaps: The bill requires agencies to notify denied applicants of the basis for security-related rejections but provides no appeal or reconsideration process for small businesses that dispute a watchlist-based determination.

Strategic breakthrough allocations target "critical technology areas" but the bill does not define or enumerate those areas, leaving the scope of the new allocation category entirely to agency discretion.

added: Requirement for SBIR and STTR agencies to evaluate security risks of applicants through watchlist screening, intelligence community coordination, and classified risk assessment
Eight-watchlist disqualification framework for SBIR and STTR applicants with foreign adversary connections
Notification requirement for security-based denials, to the extent consistent with national security
Maximum proposal cap per small business per fiscal year for Phase I and Phase II solicitations
Strategic breakthrough allocations — additional Phase II awards for critical technology areas requiring matching private funds
modified: SBIR and STTR program authorization extended through fiscal year 2031
Phase III commercialization training requirements for agency contracting officers expanded
